Messages.Author: Ped Xing
Messages.Body:
So... I am looking for some advice from the seasoned players out there
that have attended lots of tournaments and conventions and have played
VTES with a wider group of players than their local weekly game...

I've noticed that my decks tend to be highly (HIGHLY) tuned to destroy
tables for my local meta-game here in Tucson, but when I head up to
Phoenix for tournaments, the best I've been able to do is 2nd place in
any tournament. Now obviously this can't all be blamed on the deck I
play and how it's tuned of course; Fred especially as well as Ben and
Scott and the other Phoenix guys are some skilled players and deserved
their wins. But what I want to learn to do is tune my decks for a more
general metagame, so I can take them to Phoenix, or really any
tournament or metagame in the U.S., and be able to stand a chance at
CONSISTENTLY getting some V.P.'s.

So, is there a deck building strategy that those of you out there use
to adjust your decks to a more general meta-game? Should decks be more
tool-boxy? Is there a way to anticipate a tournament meta-game
beforehand?

Thanks in advance,
Matt

Messages.Author: d...@petsparc.mc.duke.edu
Messages.Body:
On 22 Jan 2003, Ped Xing wrote:

> So, is there a deck building strategy that those of you out there use
> to adjust your decks to a more general meta-game? Should decks be more
> tool-boxy? Is there a way to anticipate a tournament meta-game
> beforehand?

If you can, build your decks to look innocuous, then go for the one-turn
kill. Realize that, unlike your local playgroup, your opponenents in a
tournament are not going to know what your deck can do unless it's a
hyperfocused, mono-discipline affair, or you are adhering tightly to a
well-known archtype ("Law Firm", Malk S+B, et al.).

Look for cards, or clusters of cards, that can address several game
elements at once. Auspex has some good dual-use intercept, FOR has
dual-use prevention, Dominate and Presence have dual-use bleed
actions. Bloodlines has lots of this sort of thing, if you happen to be
playing a deck that can benefit from it. Chimestry has nothing like this,
though. Forget Chimestry.

Try to choose vampires that have specials that support or compliment your
strategy. A special, if it's good enough and you can see it hit the
table, translates directly into freed-up card slots, and you can use those
slots to painlessly diversify *or* focus even more on having your needed
cards in hand, as you wish.

Play eighty card decks and don't double up so much on the good
mastercards. There are good arguments against this, but that's the side
of the fence I'm on. I've been playing eighty card decks for at least a
year now, and there does seem to be a noticeable improvement in draw and
reliability.

Play weenies. Or Dominate. Or both.

David Cherryholmes
Prince of Durham, NC

I agree, this is good advice.

Beyond what David has said, I'd add that there is very little
difference between second place and first place. Yeah, the
winning deck list doesn't think so, but in my experience, if
you're good enough to come in second, you're also good enough
to win - things just didn't work out in your favor. :-)

If things never work out in your favor after 5+ times you've
made the final round, then it may be that something is going
on - that you're telegraphing your dangerousness too much, or
something. And having a deck with the element of surprise is
always nice - one that people have never seen anything like
it before, or at least one that does surprising things, as
David was saying. But overall, I think that if your decks
are doing well enough to make the finals, there's probably no
diagnosable reason that you haven't won with them - just not
lucky, yet.

Josh

Messages.Author: Halcyan 2
Messages.Body:
>But is that necessarily a bad thing?

In my opinion, yes.

>On the face of it, it would definitely
>seem a little shady, but I don't know if it wouldn't make for some more
>interesting tournaments. For one thing, it would serve to un-wallpaper a
>lot of cards. It would also introduce a new kind of strategy to the
>tournament scene. It's not as if you, as the Tzimisce Deck, wouldn't also
>have the opportunity to slide in some Cultivated Blood Shortages or Whispers
>of the Nictuku or something. I don't really have much of an idea as to the
>finer details of how sideboards work in other games (i.e. how big your side
>board is allowed to be, etc...), but it might be interesting if done
>properly.
>

Well, one of the most important and critical aspects of deck-building is how
you deal with other deck archetypes.

Some decks might decide to go more toolboxy. Passing on something more focused
so that they'd be able to deal with a wider range of situations. Other decks
might pack some defense (S:CE, Delaying Tactics, Wakes) in case they need it,
but if you don't end up using it it just clogs their hand. And finally there
are some decks that just say "screw it" and don't bother with defense. Some
decks designed to go forward at full-strength don't bother with Wakes or other
reactions. Some decks might just pass on combat defense. Etc.

Choosing which path you will take is an important decision (and one that will
potentially help or hinder you).

Sideboards make things too easy. When you build your deck, you should build it
to be able to deal with somethings and build it knowing that it can't deal with
others (whether because you choose not to build it that way or because some
deck types always get screwed over by others).

Letting the fattie vote deck swap out all his combat defense (since know one's
playing combat) and put in some Rabble Razings and Ancilla Empowerments to
counter the weenie hordes isn't a good idea IMO. Nor is letting the Toreador
vote deck ditch the intercept (since no one's playing s&b) and throw in some
Justicar Retributions since there's going to be an IC deck at the table. The
weenie Potence deck sees the Cailean Trap deck and decides to swap in 10 Sewer
Lids. Etc, etc.

As I pointed out before, it eliminates the opportunity cost for many of the
potentially powerful but more cornercase cards and also takes away an important
choice in deck-building.

Halcyan 2

"Peter Oh" <ohb...@wam.umd.edu> wrote in message news:<p7NX9.126043$hK4.10...@bgtnsc05-news.ops.worldnet.att.net>...

> For one thing, it would serve to un-wallpaper a lot of cards.

At what cost, though? This isn't like the un-wallpapering of Oxford
University. The cards that you're un-wallpapering can completely hose
a player's game, all because they chose the "wrong" clan to play when
someone happened to be packing that clanhoser. You're introducing
even more randomness and game imbalance with no clear benefit other
than making a few cards useful.

> It would also introduce a new kind of strategy to the tournament scene.
> It's not as if you, as the Tzimisce Deck, wouldn't also
> have the opportunity to slide in some Cultivated Blood Shortages or Whispers
> of the Nictuku or something.

There's been times where a clan hoser has shown up in a deck list
(usually Malk Dementia). But as other people have said, that's an
opportunity risk that you'll just have to take. Take away the
opportunity cost away and it becomes "who happens to have the right
clanhoser in their sideboard and who draws it at the right time".
That seems to be introducing more luck, not more strategy.

-Snapcase

Messages.Author: Ped Xing
Messages.Body:
Regarding "side-boards," my own obersvation is that, at least to some
extent, playing with the same local meta-game week-to-week is like
having/using side-boards allready in place. After consistent and
repeated play with the same people, a player starts to know what decks
his opposition plays, as well as any specific playing styles and
strategies. Thus, in the long term, the same kind of deck-tweaking
occurs that might occur between rounds in a tournament that uses
side-boarding.

But this happens occasionally on an even on a larger, wider scale.
Case in point: take a look at David Cherryholmes' "Big Hair, Bad
Attitude" deck posted on this NG
(http://groups.google.com/groups?dq=&hl=en&lr=&ie=UTF-8&selm=Pine.GSO.4.21.0301211231190.1545-100000%40petsparc.mc.duke.edu)
in which he freely admits that his intention is to survive Peter's
inevitable weenie potence horde in Boston. David's advantage is that
he posseses the foreknowledge that the Nosferatu hate him (they hate
everybody!) and has "side-boarded" an entire deck which he hopes will
disrupt a strategy in that specific meta-game.

Is it a mistake on Peter's part that the Nosferatu are so vocal in
their hatred that they will allow other players to anticipate their
wrath? My own understanding is that a "Spanish Inquisition"**
technique is preferable in the wider meta-game. Or is a fearsome
confidence in your deck and your playing ability a far more powerful
tool? In order to adjust to the wider meta-game, is it a "mental"
tweaking that's required rather than a deck tweaking?

Thanks in advance to all responses,
Matt

(**btw, by "Spanish Inquisition," I mean, "fear, surprise, ruthless
efficiency, an almost fanatical devotion to the Pope, and nice red
uniforms").

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <RH1Y9.11229$LA4.5...@news1.west.cox.net>, Kevin M.

<you...@imaspammer.org> writes:
>Red herring: Magic was DESIGNED as a CL game.

Pedantry: No it wasn't.

Magic was *later* altered to be a CL game. It is probably true that all
revisions post the introduction of the CL regarded it as *only* a CL
game.

The 20 Mountains, 40 Lightning Bolt deck (and similar) is mostly *why*
the CL was introduced.

Jyhad was designed knowing this. Hence Jyhad has many rules in place
(no repeat action modifiers, no repeat reactions, no excess stealth, no
excess intercept, no useless maneuvers, no useless presses, - later on,
no repeat actions, and its current version) and many concepts in place
(vampires->actions, so combat can take out actions, jamming a deck)
which made the lack of a card limit entirely possible.

But Magic wasn't designed with a CL. Richard Garfield assumed no-one
would ever get a full set, and that 400 cards would be a *lot* of cards
for one player to have. (This is also why balancing cards through
rarity is bad.) It was designed as a fun, knockabout game.

--

> Beyond what David has said, I'd add that there is very little
> difference between second place and first place. Yeah, the

>

> <snip>

>
> But overall, I think that if your decks are doing well enough
> to make the finals, there's probably no diagnosable reason that
> you haven't won with them - just not lucky, yet.

AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA!!!!!!

No!!!!!

There is a BIG difference between first place and second place.
Certain types of decks - particularly intercept-combat walls -
are great at coming in second place at a table (and tournaments)
but are absolutely horrible at coming in first place. I can't
count the number of times I've witnessed players - particularly
in the pre-Table-Wins Era - approach a tournament with the
attitude of "If I just get 2 VP per round, then I'll make the
finals, and then I'll have a shot at winning!", only to lose in
the finals - in second place.

Mind you, there are a lot of players out there who are just fine
with coming in second place a lot, 'cause it's not a bad track
record at all. However, there are probably at least as many who
see that track record as a sign that they're on the right track
towards winning tournaments, and if they just keep at it they'll
eventually get it right and start winning tournaments regularly.

The fact of the matter is that second place decks are only good
at coming in second place, and while they might win a tournament
once in a blue moon (it's happened), they realistically can't
expect to do any better than second. First place decks, on the
other hand, may come in second place at times, may come in first
place at times, and may flame out entirely. However, they at least
give themselves a realistic shot of winning a game.

- Ben Peal, Prince of Boston

I'm not sure I agree. Though what I was talking about was second
place in a *tournament* not second place in a single game, which
might be why you're objecting. Yes, in any game, obviously first
is better than second. But if you're doing well enough in
tournaments to make the finals and come in second overall, you're
probably not playing an "always comes in second" deck.

As James Coupe pointed out, in the post-TW era, in tournaments
of any size, you can't get to the finals without having earned
some game wins in the prelim rounds. So if your deck is totally
unable to do better than second place, it's not going to even
make the finals, let alone get second place in the finals. All
the people it lost to in the first three rounds will be ahead of
it. :-)

I'll agree that some decks have a harder time getting to 3 VPs
than others, especially wall-type decks. But in individual
games as well as tournaments, I see a lot more randomness than
we might like to admit, and that can certainly lead to walls
getting game wins and even tournament wins.

They're annoying to play against, and if played badly can be
very ineffective at winning and "screw up" the dynamics of the
table. But the same can be said of a lot of decktypes, by no
means excluding the "never does anything but hurt my prey" type.

Josh

Messages.Author: Ben Peal

James Coupe:

> Ben Peal wrote:
> > Certain types of decks - particularly intercept-combat walls -
> > are great at coming in second place at a table (and tournaments)
> > but are absolutely horrible at coming in first place. I can't
> > count the number of times I've witnessed players - particularly
> > in the pre-Table-Wins Era - approach a tournament with the
> > attitude of "If I just get 2 VP per round, then I'll make the
> > finals, and then I'll have a shot at winning!", only to lose in
> > the finals - in second place.
>
> If they're coming in second place and getting 2VPs, they're not getting
> a table win - someone else must have got more than 2VPs (they're in
> second) and therefore got a table win.
>
> A deck that manages 0 table wins and 6 VPs is unlikely to reach the
> final, in most tournaments.

Thank you, Captain Obvious.

What the intercept-combat wall decks would try to do is be the
last man standing in a given round. That way they'd get 2 VP,
and occasionally get a win if nobody else got more than 1 VP.
They might even occasionally oust someone earlier on, too. In
the PRE-TABLE-WINS-ERA, as I mentioned above and which was
scarcely more than a year ago, this was a very common approach,
and in my opinion stunted the player's development as they had
a hard time breaking out of their brain lock and learning how
to actually win a game. What caused the unwillingness to break
out of playing intercept-combat was the perception that they
were _almost_ there...that since they were coming in 2nd place
so much, and were _in_ every game so much that they must be
doing something right and they should just stick with it and
refine it, never realizing that they had hit a wall.

In the Table Wins Era, yes, intercept-combat wall decks have
become less common, but they do still exist. They still get
2nd place at a table with the same regularity. They still
might get a Table Win on occasion if they're the last deck
standing and nobody gets more than 1 VP. Hell, they might
even get an oust earlier in the game. On those occasions when
they get a Table Win, there's a good chance that they'll make
the finals, and then inevitably come in 2nd place in the finals.

And if you tell them to try something else, they'll point at
the few intercept-combat wall decks that were lucky enough to
win a tournament. How did they win? If you can occasionally
get a Table Win in the preliminary rounds, then occasionally
you might get a Table Win in the finals. So, once in a blue
moon upon a blue moon, an intercept-wall deck might win.

So, the difficulty a new player can have with assessing their
decks and strategy is that they might not know when they're
hitting a wall, and when they're actually onto something that
could win them a tournament with some development. If the
advice is simply, "Hey, you took second place! You're almost
there!", you might be doing them more harm than good.



(Thanks, by the way. But I agree with Josh - I won that tournament by the
thinnest of margins and got some pretty meaningful breaks along the way.
Such as in the finals when Scott used his Archon Investigation to burn
Ben's vampire that I'd bounced to him. _That_ doesn't happen every day...)

I've been exactly where you are but substitute, "Able to win in Phoenix"
and then go to LA or Gencon and would get totally trashed. My answer to
this is to go to LA and Gencon as much as I possibly can. Get your butt
kicked, but do so with your eyes open. Notice what other people do to
you that hurts. That both give you the option of picking up the same
techniques and figuring out how to resist them.

intercept, and bounce in my deck. This may not come as a shock to folks
on this forum, but I guess I was just ignoring these too much in my decks
and building things that just couldn't win against good competition. I
think you can win without any of them but I'm not very good with rush combat
and any other deck ideas had better be damn good or you'll pay too much.
Anyway, that was just my little experience. Your own may be different.

Fred
